citation.title: Interval Estimation of Population Means under Unknown but Bounded Probabilities of Sample Selection

standing_assumptions:
Finite-population (design-based) sampling setting; every probability is over the sampling design. Transcribed from the page images of main.pdf (Biometrika 100(1), 235-240; printed page = PDF page + 234). The proof of Proposition 1 is in the Appendix (pp. 239-240, PDF pp. 5-6); the proofs of Lemma 1 and of Propositions 2 and 3 are in the official supplement (staged/supplements/Bka-12-198_supplement.pdf, 2 pp., cited below as 'Supplement p. 1/2').

(S1) Population, sample, ordering, estimand [Section 2, p. 235 (PDF p. 1)]: 'Consider a population $U$ indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, N$, with associated responses $y_i \in \mathbb{R}$. Let $I_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is sampled from the population; otherwise, let $I_i = 0$. Under a given sampling design, the probability of $i$ being selected is $\pi_i$, so that $\mathrm{pr}(I_i = 1) = \pi_i$. Without loss of generality, assume an index ordering such that the first $n$ units are the sampled units and the remaining $N - n$ are the unsampled units; that is, $I_i = 1$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$ and $I_i = 0$ for $i = n+1, \ldots, N$, so that the set of sampled units is $S = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Further, let the units in $S$ be ordered so that $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$. The goal is to estimate the population mean, $\mu = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i/N$.'

(S2) Horvitz-Thompson and Hajek estimators [Section 2, pp. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)]: 'When the probabilities of sample selection are known, and if $\pi_i > 0$ for all $i$, then the Horvitz-Thompson estimator of $\mu$, $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (I_i y_i)/(N\pi_i)$, is unbiased. Similarly, we can define a random variable that has expectation 1: $\hat 1_{\mathrm{HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} I_i/(N\pi_i)$. The Hajek (1971) ratio estimator of $\mu$ is then $\hat\mu = \dfrac{\hat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}}{\hat 1_{\mathrm{HT}}} = \dfrac{\sum_{i\in S}\pi_i^{-1}y_i}{\sum_{i\in S}\pi_i^{-1}} = \dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n}$, (1) where $w = (w_1, \ldots, w_n) = (\pi_1^{-1}, \ldots, \pi_n^{-1})$, $y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)$, and $1_n$ is an $n$-vector of ones.'

(S3) Bounded probabilities and the two optimisation problems [Section 3.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 2)]: 'Suppose that we no longer have exact knowledge of the sampling design, instead knowing only that $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$ for all $i$. While consistent point estimation is no longer possible without further assumptions, it is possible to obtain an interval estimate for $\mu$. In fact, sharp bounds for the Hajek estimator (1) exist, in the sense that the set of all possible values of $\hat\mu$ is precisely the interval $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}]$. If $\pi_i \in [\alpha, \beta]$, an upper bound on $\hat\mu$ is $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = \max_w\left\{\dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n} : 1/\beta \leqslant w_1, \ldots, w_n \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (2) Likewise, a lower bound is $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \min_w\left\{\dfrac{w'y}{w'1_n} : 1/\beta \leqslant w_1, \ldots, w_n \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (3)' The ratio $\gamma$ is introduced in Proposition 1 (p. 236): 'Let $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ be the relative magnitude of $\beta$ compared to $\alpha$.'

(S4) Brewer scaling [Section 3.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]: 'The proposed interval estimator yields asymptotically sharp bounds on $\mu$ itself under the scaling proposed by Brewer (1979) and articulated in Assumption 1.' 'Assumption 1. The sequences of finite populations $\{U_h\}_{h=1}^{\infty}$ and samples $\{S_h\}_{h=1}^{\infty}$ grow as follows. For each $h \geqslant 1$, $U_h = \{U_{h-1}, U\} = \{U, \ldots, U\}$, i.e., $U_h$ consists of $h$ replicates of the original population $U$, so that $|U_h| = hN$. For each $h$, a sample $s_h$ is drawn from $U$ according to the original sampling design, independent of $s_1, \ldots, s_{h-1}$; hence $S_h = \{S_{h-1}, s_h\} = \{s_1, \ldots, s_h\}$. The estimators $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ follow equations (2) and (3), respectively, but applied to the population $U_h$ and the sample $S_h$.'

(S5) Outcome classes, class totals, the limiting optimisation problems [Section 3.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]: 'Let $Y$ be the ordered set of distinct outcomes in $U$, so that $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(|Y|)}$, with equivalence classes $\Upsilon_j \equiv \{i = 1, \ldots, N : y_i = y_{(j)}\}$. In the limit of the Brewer scaling, the probabilities $\pi_i$ can be identified up to units with identical outcomes: as $h \to \infty$, $(\sum_{\{i=1,\ldots,Nh : y_i = y_{(j)}\}} I_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^{Nh} I_i) \to \Pi_j/(\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k)$ where $\Pi_j = \sum_{i\in\Upsilon_j}\pi_i$. Since $\pi_i \geqslant \alpha > 0$ for all $i$, $Y$ is identified in the limit. If $W_j \equiv |\Upsilon_j|/\Pi_j$ is known for all $j = 1, \ldots, |Y|$, then $\mu$ is identified: $\mu = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j \frac{\Pi_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k} y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\frac{\Pi_j}{\sum_{k=1}^{|Y|}\Pi_k}}$. However, $W_j$ is actually only identified up to the interval $\beta^{-1} \leqslant W_j \leqslant \alpha^{-1}$; so in the limit, $\mu$ can be identified up to the interval bounded by $\mu_+ = \max_W\left\{\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} : 1/\beta \leqslant W_1, \ldots, W_{|Y|} \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$ (6) and $\mu_- = \min_W\left\{\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|} W_j\Pi_j} : 1/\beta \leqslant W_1, \ldots, W_{|Y|} \leqslant 1/\alpha\right\}$. (7)'

(S6) Assumption 2 [Section 3.2, p. 238 (PDF p. 4)], preceded by: 'By Proposition 2, if $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h \to \mu_+$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h \to \mu_-$ as $h \to \infty$, then $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h]$ is asymptotically sharp. A mild technical condition on $k_+$ and $k_-$ is necessary to guarantee convergence.' 'Assumption 2. For any $k \geqslant 0$, $y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, $\quad y_{(k+1)} \neq \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$.'

(S7) Reading conventions; these are not printed. They are the ones the validators fixed (validated.json, natural_reading fields) and every target uses them. (a) $n \geqslant 1$, $|Y| \geqslant 1$, and an empty sum is $0$. (b) A rule of the form 'the smallest nonnegative integer $k$ that satisfies [...] $y_{k+1}$' ranges over the integers $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1$, the only $k$ for which $y_{k+1}$ is defined; likewise $0 \leqslant k \leqslant |Y|-1$ for a rule in $y_{(k+1)}$ and for Assumption 2. (c) The objective of (2)-(3) is unchanged when $w$ is multiplied by a positive constant, so with $u = \beta w$ the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$ becomes $[1, \gamma]^n$. For $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n$ write $F^{\mathrm H}_k = \{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{k + \gamma(n-k)\}$ and $F^{\mathrm L}_k = \{\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{\gamma k + (n-k)\}$: these are the values of $w'y/(w'1_n)$ at the threshold vectors $w^{k}$ (first $k$ entries $1/\beta$, last $n-k$ entries $1/\alpha$; Appendix, p. 239) and (first $k$ entries $1/\alpha$, last $n-k$ entries $1/\beta$), respectively. The same holds with class totals: for $0 \leqslant k \leqslant |Y|$, $G^{+}_k = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$ and $G^{-}_k = \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$ are the values of the objective of (6)-(7) at the threshold vectors (first $k$ entries $1/\beta$, rest $1/\alpha$) and (first $k$ entries $1/\alpha$, rest $1/\beta$). (d) $\Pi_j > 0$ for every $j$, because each class $\Upsilon_j$ is nonempty and $\pi_i \geqslant \alpha > 0$; hence every denominator in (6), (7) and in $G^{\pm}_k$ is positive. (e) In Section 3.2 the estimators $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ are (2) and (3) computed from the pooled sample $S_h$ (all sampled units of the $h$ replicates); they are defined when $S_h$ is nonempty.

(S8) Transcription notes (checked on 420 dpi crops of the page images). (a) In (5) and in the dichotomous display the left-hand set is printed with $\pi_N$ (capital $N$), although $\hat\mu$ depends only on $\pi_1, \ldots, \pi_n$. (b) Proposition 3 prints $\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$ and $\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$ without hats; the sentence two lines above it and Assumption 1 print $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H}_h$, $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}_h$. (c) In Proposition 2 the two second sums of the $\mu_-$ display are printed with lower limit $j = k_- - 1$; every other display of the paper has $k+1$ there. (d) The rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$ (p. 236) and the rule for $k_-$ (p. 238, directly below Table 1) are both printed with $\geqslant$; the rules for $k^{\mathrm H}$ and $k_+$ with $\leqslant$. (e) The supplement sets the superscripts H and L in italic and writes $\leq$, $\geq$; the article sets them upright and writes $\leqslant$, $\geqslant$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1, second half (the rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$, the lower optimiser $w^{\mathrm L}$ and the lower bound $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}$), as printed: a two-unit sample in which the printed rule gives $1/2$ while the minimum of (3) is $1/3$
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement refuted: Proposition 1, p. 236 (PDF p. 2)] 'An optimal solution to (3) is $w^{\mathrm L} = (1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha, 1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta)$, where the first $k^{\mathrm L}$ entries equal $1/\alpha$ and the remaining $n - k^{\mathrm L}$ entries equal $1/\beta$, with $k^{\mathrm L}$ being the smallest nonnegative integer $k$ that satisfies $\{\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{\gamma k + (n-k)\} \geqslant y_{k+1}$. The lower bound on $\hat\mu$ is therefore $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{k^{\mathrm L}} y_i + \sum_{i=k^{\mathrm L}+1}^{n} y_i}{\gamma k^{\mathrm L} + (n-k^{\mathrm L})}$.' [Counterexample from the validators (validate/P025-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 2; v2/artifact/derivation.md, section 3); not in the paper.] $n = 2$, $y = (y_1, y_2) = (0, 1)$, $\alpha = 1/2$, $\beta = 1$, so $\gamma = \beta/\alpha = 2$. (a) [The hypotheses hold.] $0 < \alpha \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, $\gamma = 2 \geqslant 1$, $n \geqslant 1$ and $y_1 \leqslant y_2$. (The sample is realizable: a two-unit population with outcomes $(0,1)$ and independent inclusion probabilities $(1/2, 1)$ yields this sample with probability $1/2$.) (b) [The printed rule returns $k^{\mathrm L} = 0$.] At $k = 0$ the left side of the printed test is $\{\gamma\cdot 0 + (0+1)\}/\{\gamma\cdot 0 + 2\} = 1/2$ and $1/2 \geqslant y_1 = 0$; $0$ is the smallest nonnegative integer. (c) [What the proposition then asserts.] $w^{\mathrm L} = (1/\beta, 1/\beta) = (1, 1)$ (no entry equals $1/\alpha$) and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = (y_1 + y_2)/2 = 1/2$. (d) [The assertion is false.] Problem (3) is $\min\{w_2/(w_1+w_2) : 1 \leqslant w_1, w_2 \leqslant 2\}$. The feasible vector $w = (1/\alpha, 1/\beta) = (2, 1)$ gives $1/(2+1) = 1/3 < 1/2$, so the printed $w^{\mathrm L}$ is not an optimal solution to (3) and the printed $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}$ is not the minimum (3). (e) [The minimum of (3), over the whole box.] For all real $1 \leqslant w_1, w_2 \leqslant 2$: $\dfrac{w_2}{w_1+w_2} - \dfrac13 = \dfrac{(2 - w_1) + 2(w_2 - 1)}{3(w_1+w_2)} \geqslant 0$, with equality at $(w_1, w_2) = (2, 1)$. So the minimum (3) equals $1/3$, and the printed lower bound exceeds it by $1/6$. (f) [Consequence for (5).] The maximum (2) equals $2/3$: $\dfrac23 - \dfrac{w_2}{w_1+w_2} = \dfrac{2(w_1 - 1) + (2 - w_2)}{3(w_1+w_2)} \geqslant 0$, with equality at $(1, 2)$; the printed rule for $k^{\mathrm H}$ gives $k^{\mathrm H} = 1$ (at $k=0$: $1/2 \leqslant 0$ fails; at $k=1$: $(0 + 2\cdot 1)/(1+2) = 2/3 \leqslant y_2 = 1$) and (4) gives $2/3$. Hence the set of all possible values of $\hat\mu$ is $[1/3, 2/3]$, whereas the right side of (5) evaluated with the printed $k^{\mathrm L} = 0$ is $[1/2, 2/3]$, which omits the attainable values in $[1/3, 1/2)$. (g) [Why the printed rule always stops at zero; general, for every sorted sample and every $\gamma \geqslant 1$.] At $k = 0$ the left side of the printed test is the sample mean $\bar y = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i/n$, and $\bar y - y_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - y_1)/n \geqslant 0$; so the printed rule returns $k^{\mathrm L} = 0$, $w^{\mathrm L} = (1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta)$ and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \bar y$ for every data set. If $\gamma > 1$ and the $y_i$ are not all equal, $\bar y$ is not the minimum (3): changing $w_1$ alone from $1/\beta$ to $1/\alpha$ changes the objective by $(\gamma - 1)(y_1 - \bar y)/\{n + (\gamma - 1)\} < 0$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 2, the rule for $k_-$ and 'The optimal solution to (7) is $W_-$', as printed: a two-class population in which the printed $W_-$ gives $2/3$ while the minimum of (7), and the population mean, is $1/2$
canonical_claim.location: p. 238 (PDF p. 4), directly below Table 1; (7) on p. 237 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed statement refuted: Proposition 2, p. 238 (PDF p. 4)] 'and $k_-$ is the smallest nonnegative integer $k$ satisfying $\dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j} \geqslant y_{(k+1)}$. [...] The optimal solution to (7) is $W_- = (1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha, 1/ eta, \ldots, 1/ eta)$, where the first $k_-$ entries equal $1/\alpha$ and the remaining $|Y| - k_-$ entries equal $1/ eta$.' [Counterexample from the validator (validate/P025-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 3); not in the paper.] Population $U$ of $N = 2$ units with outcomes $(y_1, y_2) = (0, 1)$; the design includes unit 2 always and unit 1 with probability $1/2$, so $(\pi_1, \pi_2) = (1/2, 1)$. Take $\alpha = 1/2$, $ eta = 1$, $\gamma = 2$. (a) [The hypotheses hold.] $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant  eta \leqslant 1$ for both units; $Y = (0, 1)$, $|Y| = 2$, $y_{(1)} = 0 < y_{(2)} = 1$, $\Upsilon_1 = \{1\}$, $\Upsilon_2 = \{2\}$, $(\Pi_1, \Pi_2) = (1/2, 1)$; independent replication of this design gives Assumption 1. The population mean is $\mu = 1/2$ and the true class weights are $(W_1, W_2) = (|\Upsilon_1|/\Pi_1, |\Upsilon_2|/\Pi_2) = (2, 1)$. (b) [The printed rule returns $k_- = 0$.] At $k = 0$ the left side is $(\Pi_1\cdot 0 + \Pi_2\cdot 1)/(\Pi_1 + \Pi_2) = 1/(3/2) = 2/3 \geqslant y_{(1)} = 0$. (c) [What the proposition then asserts.] $W_- = (1/ eta, 1/ eta) = (1, 1)$ is 'the optimal solution to (7)'; the objective of (7) at $W_- = (1,1)$ is $2/3$. (d) [The assertion is false.] With $u = W_1$, $v = W_2$, the objective of (7) is $v/(u/2 + v)$ on $1 \leqslant u, v \leqslant 2$. At $(u, v) = (1/\alpha, 1/ eta) = (2, 1)$ it equals $1/2 < 2/3$. For all real $1 \leqslant u, v \leqslant 2$: $\dfrac{v}{u/2+v} - \dfrac12 = \dfrac{(2-u) + 2(v-1)}{2(u+2v)} \geqslant 0$, with equality at $(2, 1)$; so the minimum (7) is $\mu_- = 1/2$, not $2/3$. (e) [The printed 'lower bound' is not a lower bound on $\mu$.] The value $2/3$ delivered by the printed rule exceeds the population mean $\mu = 1/2$. (f) [Upper half, for comparison.] The maximum (6) is $4/5$: $\dfrac45 - \dfrac{v}{u/2+v} = \dfrac{4(u-1) + 2(2-v)}{5(u+2v)} \geqslant 0$, with equality at $(1, 2)$; the printed rule gives $k_+ = 1$ ($k=0$: $2/3 \leqslant 0$ fails; $k = 1$: $(\Pi_1\cdot 0 + \gamma\Pi_2\cdot 1)/(\Pi_1 + \gamma\Pi_2) = 2/(5/2) = 4/5 \leqslant 1$) and $\mu_+ = 4/5$. (g) [Assumption 2 does not remove the defect.] At $k = 0$ both expressions of Assumption 2 equal $2/3 
eq y_{(1)} = 0$; at $k = 1$ they equal $4/5 
eq 1$ and $1/2 
eq 1$. (h) [General, for all class totals $\Pi_j > 0$ and all $\gamma \geqslant 1$.] At $k = 0$ the left side of the printed test is the $\Pi$-weighted mean $\sum_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j\Pi_j \geqslant y_{(1)}$, so the printed rule always returns $k_- = 0$ and $W_- = (1/ eta, \ldots, 1/ eta)$; if $\gamma > 1$ and $|Y| \geqslant 2$ this vector does not minimise (7). (With $k_- = 0$ the printed $\mu_-$ display has tail sums starting at $j = -1$, which is not a class index; this is the separate finding P025-E002, targets P025-T9 and P025-T10. Parts (c)-(e) use (7) and the printed $W_-$ only.)

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1 and equation (5), corrected: $\leqslant$ in the rule for $k^{\mathrm L}$
canonical_claim.location: p. 236 (PDF p. 2); proof in the Appendix, pp. 239-240 (PDF pp. 5-6), which omits the lower half ('The solution to (3) can be derived in a similar manner.')
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected statement. The printed one is Proposition 1 with equation (5), p. 236 (PDF p. 2), transcribed in P025-T7. The single change is $\leqslant$ for $\geqslant$ in the rule that defines $k^{\mathrm L}$ (Sol's smallest repair, validated.json, P025-E001: 'Replace >= by <= in the k^L definition in Proposition 1 and the k_- definition in Proposition 2. Optionally make their existing valid search ranges explicit as 0<=k<n and 0<=k<|Y|; the last valid index always qualifies.'). The search range, implicit in the printed $y_{k+1}$, is written out. No hypothesis is added.] PROPOSITION 1 (corrected). Let $n \geqslant 1$, let $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$ be real, let $0 < \alpha \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$ and let $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ be the relative magnitude of $\beta$ compared to $\alpha$. An optimal solution to (2) is $w^{\mathrm H} = (1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta, 1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$, where the first $k^{\mathrm H}$ entries equal $1/\beta$ and the remaining $n - k^{\mathrm H}$ entries equal $1/\alpha$, with $k^{\mathrm H}$ being the smallest integer $k \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ that satisfies $\{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{k + \gamma(n-k)\} \leqslant y_{k+1}$. The upper bound on $\hat\mu$ is therefore $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k^{\mathrm H}} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k^{\mathrm H}+1}^{n} y_i}{k^{\mathrm H} + \gamma(n-k^{\mathrm H})}$. (4) An optimal solution to (3) is $w^{\mathrm L} = (1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha, 1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta)$, where the first $k^{\mathrm L}$ entries equal $1/\alpha$ and the remaining $n - k^{\mathrm L}$ entries equal $1/\beta$, with $k^{\mathrm L}$ being the smallest integer $k \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ that satisfies $\{\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i\}/\{\gamma k + (n-k)\} \leqslant y_{k+1}$. The lower bound on $\hat\mu$ is therefore $\hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{k^{\mathrm L}} y_i + \sum_{i=k^{\mathrm L}+1}^{n} y_i}{\gamma k^{\mathrm L} + (n-k^{\mathrm L})}$. With these $k^{\mathrm L}$ and $k^{\mathrm H}$, $[\hat\mu^{\mathrm L}, \hat\mu^{\mathrm H}]$ is the set of all possible values of $\hat\mu$: $\{\hat\mu : \alpha \leqslant \pi_1, \ldots, \pi_N \leqslant \beta\} = \left[\dfrac{\gamma\sum_{i=1}^{k^{\mathrm L}} y_i + \sum_{i=k^{\mathrm L}+1}^{n} y_i}{\gamma k^{\mathrm L} + (n-k^{\mathrm L})},\ \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k^{\mathrm H}} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k^{\mathrm H}+1}^{n} y_i}{k^{\mathrm H} + \gamma(n-k^{\mathrm H})}\right]$. (5)

[Formal content, each part of the target; $F^{\mathrm H}_k$, $F^{\mathrm L}_k$ as in (S7c).] Let $B = [1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$ and $R(w) = w'y/(w'1_n)$ for $w \in B$ (the denominator is positive). (a) [The cut points exist.] $F^{\mathrm H}_{n-1} \leqslant y_n$ and $F^{\mathrm L}_{n-1} \leqslant y_n$ (each is an average of $y_1, \ldots, y_n$ with positive weights), so both index sets are nonempty. (b) [Values at the threshold vectors.] $R(w^{\mathrm H}) = F^{\mathrm H}_{k^{\mathrm H}}$ and $R(w^{\mathrm L}) = F^{\mathrm L}_{k^{\mathrm L}}$, and $w^{\mathrm H}, w^{\mathrm L} \in B$. canonical_claim.statement: [Printed, pp. 238-239 (PDF pp. 4-5)] 'The estimates for the shooting gallery and needle exchange populations overlap only when $\gamma > 3$; the estimates for the street needle and needle exchange populations overlap when $\gamma > 1{\cdot}25$. This means that for the shooting gallery needles to possibly show the same HIV prevalence rate as the exchange needles, infected shooting gallery needles must have been more than three times as likely to be tested than uninfected shooting gallery needles, with the converse holding for exchange needles.' [The claim refuted, as a statement; the validators' natural reading.] Two populations of needles with outcomes in $\{0, 1\}$ (1 = infected), gallery ($G$) and exchange ($E$), sampled with inclusion probabilities bounded as in (S3), yield the reported samples: 48 tested with 91·7% positive, and 579 tested with 50·3% positive. If the two population prevalences are equal, then both $r_G > 3$ and $r_E > 3$, where $r_G = \pi_{G,1}/\pi_{G,0}$ is the ratio of the selection probability of an infected gallery needle to that of an uninfected one and $r_E = \pi_{E,0}/\pi_{E,1}$ is the reverse ratio for exchange needles. [Counterexamples from the validator (validate/P025-E003/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 4-6); not in the paper.] In each population the design draws, independently in each infection stratum, a uniformly random subset of fixed size; a unit's inclusion probability is the stratum sample size divided by the stratum population size. (A) [The exchange ratio is below three.] Gallery: 48 infected and 16 uninfected needles in the population; sample 44 infected and 4 uninfected; $\pi_{G,1} = 44/48 = 11/12$, $\pi_{G,0} = 4/16 = 1/4$. Exchange: 864 infected and 288 uninfected; sample 291 infected and 288 uninfected; $\pi_{E,1} = 291/864 = 97/288$, $\pi_{E,0} = 288/288 = 1$. (i) Both population prevalences equal $3/4$: $48/64 = 864/1152 = 3/4$. (ii) The samples are the reported ones: sizes $48$ and $579$; sample proportions $44/48 = 0{\cdot}91666\ldots$ and $291/579 = 0{\cdot}50259\ldots$, which round to 91·7% and 50·3%. (iii) All four probabilities lie in $[1/4, 1]$ ($97/288 > 1/4$ since $97 > 72$), so (S3) holds with $\alpha = 1/4$, $\beta = 1$, $\gamma = 4$. (iv) $r_G = (11/12)/(1/4) = 11/3 > 3$ but $r_E = 1/(97/288) = 288/97 < 3$ (since $288 < 291$). (v) On every possible draw the Hajek estimates (1) equal the population prevalences: $\dfrac{44/(11/12)}{44/(11/12) + 4/(1/4)} = \dfrac{48}{64} = \dfrac34$ and $\dfrac{291/(97/288)}{291/(97/288) + 288/1} = \dfrac{864}{1152} = \dfrac34$. (B) [The gallery ratio is below three.] Gallery: 48 infected and 12 uninfected; sample 44 and 4; $\pi_{G,1} = 11/12$, $\pi_{G,0} = 4/12 = 1/3$. Exchange: 1156 infected and 289 uninfected; sample 291 and 288; $\pi_{E,1} = 291/1156$, $\pi_{E,0} = 288/289$. (i) Both prevalences equal $4/5$: $48/60 = 1156/1445 = 4/5$. (ii) Same samples as in (A). (iii) All four probabilities lie in $[1/4, 1]$ ($291/1156 > 1/4$ since $1164 > 1156$), so $\gamma = 4$ again. (iv) $r_G = (11/12)/(1/3) = 11/4 < 3$, while $r_E = (288/289)/(291/1156) = 384/97 > 3$. (v) The Hajek estimates are $48/60 = 4/5$ and $1156/1445 = 4/5$ on every draw. (C) [Both examples are inside the paper's intervals at $\gamma = 4$.] With $L(p, \gamma) = p/\{\gamma(1-p)+p\}$ and $H(p, \gamma) = \gamma p/\{(1-p)+\gamma p\}$: $L(11/12, 4) = 11/15 \leqslant 3/4 < 4/5 \leqslant H(97/193, 4) = 388/484 = 97/121$, so $3/4$ and $4/5$ lie in the gallery interval and in the exchange interval at $\gamma = 4$. (D) [The same with the printed rounded proportions as exact limiting selected fractions.] Common prevalence $q = 3/4$ with $\pi_{G,1} = 1$, $\pi_{G,0} = 249/917$, $\pi_{E,1} = 503/1491$, $\pi_{E,0} = 1$ (all in $[1/4, 1]$): the selected positive fractions $q\pi_1/\{q\pi_1 + (1-q)\pi_0\}$ are exactly $917/1000$ and $503/1000$, and $r_E = 1491/503 < 3$. Common prevalence $q = 4/5$ with $\pi_{G,1} = 1$, $\pi_{G,0} = 332/917$, $\pi_{E,1} = 503/1988$, $\pi_{E,0} = 1$ (all in $[1/4, 1]$): the selected fractions are again exactly $917/1000$ and $503/1000$, and $r_G = 917/332 < 3$. So equal prevalence in the two populations, with the reported samples, requires neither $r_G > 3$ nor $r_E > 3$.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected sentence; Sol's smallest repair, validated.json, P025-E003.] 'For the shooting gallery and needle exchange interval estimates to overlap, the common bound on selection-probability ratios must be at least about 3.30. This does not require both populations' actual directional selection ratios to exceed three.'

[Formal content of the corrected claim, with every hypothesis; from validate/P025-E003/v1/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2-3.] Let $L(p, \gamma) = \dfrac{p}{\gamma(1-p)+p}$ and $H(p, \gamma) = \dfrac{\gamma p}{(1-p)+\gamma p}$ be the endpoints of the dichotomous closed form (p. 237), for $0 < p < 1$ and $\gamma \geqslant 1$. (a) [Overlap criterion.] For $0 < p_E < p_G < 1$ and $\gamma \geqslant 1$, the intervals $[L(p_G, \gamma), H(p_G, \gamma)]$ and $[L(p_E, \gamma), H(p_E, \gamma)]$ intersect if and only if $L(p_G, \gamma) \leqslant H(p_E, \gamma)$, if and only if $\gamma^2 \geqslant K$, where $K = \dfrac{p_G(1-p_E)}{(1-p_G)p_E}$ is the odds ratio of the two sample proportions. (b) [The threshold for the reported proportions.] With the printed proportions $p_G = 917/1000$ and $p_E = 503/1000$: $K = \dfrac{917\cdot 497}{83\cdot 503} = \dfrac{455749}{41749}$ and $(3{\cdot}30)^2 < K < (3{\cdot}31)^2$, so the intervals overlap exactly when $\gamma \geqslant \sqrt{455749/41749} = 3{\cdot}30399\ldots$. With the proportions implied by the counts, $p_G = 44/48$ and $p_E = 291/579$: $K = 1056/97$ and $(3{\cdot}29)^2 < K < (3{\cdot}30)^2$, threshold $\sqrt{1056/97} = 3{\cdot}29948\ldots$. In both cases $9 < K < 16$: no overlap at $\gamma = 3$, overlap at $\gamma = 4$, as in Table 1. (c) [Product identity.] In a sample with positive fraction $p$ and selection probabilities $\pi_1$ for positive and $\pi_0$ for negative units ($\pi_1, \pi_0 > 0$), the Hajek estimate (1) is $q = \dfrac{p/\pi_1}{p/\pi_1 + (1-p)/\pi_0}$, and $\dfrac{q}{1-q} = \dfrac{p}{1-p}\cdot\dfrac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}$. Hence, with $r_G = \pi_{G,1}/\pi_{G,0}$ and $r_E = \pi_{E,0}/\pi_{E,1}$, the two Hajek estimates are equal if and only if $r_G\, r_E = K$. (d) [What follows, and what does not.] If the two estimates are equal and both ratios are at most a common bound $\gamma$ ($r_G \leqslant \gamma$ and $r_E \leqslant \gamma$), then $\gamma^2 \geqslant K$. The identity $r_G\, r_E = K$ does not imply $r_G > 3$, nor $r_E > 3$: $(r_G, r_E) = (11/3, 288/97)$ and $(11/4, 384/97)$ both have product $1056/97$ (P025-T5).

[pp. 237-238 (PDF pp. 3-4); the statement runs from the foot of p. 237 to below Table 1 on p. 238] 'PROPOSITION 2. In the limit $h \to \infty$, the bounds $\mu_+$ and $\mu_-$ on $\mu$ are sharp. Specifically, $\mu_+ = \dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k_+}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k_++1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k_+}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k_++1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, $\quad \mu_- = \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k_-}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k_--1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k_-}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k_--1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$, where $k_+$ is the smallest nonnegative integer $k$ satisfying $\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \gamma\sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j} \leqslant y_{(k+1)}$ and $k_-$ is the smallest nonnegative integer $k$ satisfying $\dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k+1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j} \geqslant y_{(k+1)}$. The optimal solution to (6) is $W_+ = (1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta, 1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$, where the first $k_+$ entries equal $1/\beta$ and the remaining $|Y| - k_+$ entries equal $1/\alpha$. The optimal solution to (7) is $W_- = (1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha, 1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta)$, where the first $k_-$ entries equal $1/\alpha$ and the remaining $|Y| - k_-$ entries equal $1/\beta$.'

[What the findings touch.] (i) The closed form of $\mu_+$, the rule for $k_+$ and the optimality of $W_+$ hold as printed. (ii) The rule for $k_-$ is printed with $\geqslant$ and always returns $k_- = 0$, so the asserted optimiser $W_-$ of (7) is $(1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta)$, which does not minimise (7) when $\gamma > 1$ and $|Y| \geqslant 2$ (finding P025-E001; P025-T2; corrected in P025-T4). (iii) The two second sums of the $\mu_-$ display are printed from $j = k_- - 1$ (finding P025-E002; P025-T10; corrected in P025-T9). (iv) The first sentence, 'In the limit $h \to \infty$, the bounds $\mu_+$ and $\mu_-$ on $\mu$ are sharp', is unqualified as to the information relative to which the bounds are sharp (finding P025-N002; P025-T16; corrected in P025-T15).

[Formal content, each part of the target; from validate/P025-E002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, steps 1-3.] Let $J = |Y| \geqslant 1$, $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(J)}$, $\Pi_j > 0$, $0 < \alpha \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, $\gamma = \beta/\alpha$, and let $\Phi(W) = \sum_{j=1}^{J} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}/\sum_{j=1}^{J} W_j\Pi_j$ be the objective of (7). (b) [The corrected display.] With $k_-$ the cut point of P025-T4 (the smallest $k \in \{0, \ldots, J-1\}$ with $G^{-}_k \leqslant y_{(k+1)}$), the minimum (7) equals the right side of (a) at $k = k_-$. (c) [What the printed limits do.] For $2 \leqslant k \leqslant J$, write $N_k$ and $D_k$ for the numerator and denominator in (a) and $R_k = N_k/D_k$. The printed expression, with both second sums from $j = k-1$, equals $\dfrac{N_k + \Pi_{k-1}y_{(k-1)} + \Pi_k y_{(k)}}{D_k + \Pi_{k-1} + \Pi_k}$ (classes $k-1$ and $k$ are counted in both sums) and differs from $R_k$ by $\dfrac{\Pi_{k-1}(y_{(k-1)} - R_k) + \Pi_k(y_{(k)} - R_k)}{D_k + \Pi_{k-1} + \Pi_k}$. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 2, displayed formula for $\mu_-$ with tail sums from $j = k_- - 1$, as printed: four classes in which the display evaluates to $1$ while the minimum of (7) is $7/6$
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed display refuted: Proposition 2, p. 237 (PDF p. 3)] $\mu_- = \dfrac{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k_-}\Pi_j y_{(j)} + \sum_{j=k_--1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j y_{(j)}}{\gamma\sum_{j=1}^{k_-}\Pi_j + \sum_{j=k_--1}^{|Y|}\Pi_j}$. [Counterexample from the validator (validate/P025-E002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, steps 4-7); not in the paper.] Population of six units with outcomes $(0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 3)$ and inclusion probabilities $(1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1, 1)$ (each replicate selects one of the two units with outcome 0 uniformly, one of the two units with outcome 1 uniformly, and both remaining units); $\alpha = 1/2$, $\beta = 1$, $\gamma = 2$. (a) [The hypotheses hold.] $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$; $Y = (0, 1, 2, 3)$, $|Y| = 4$; class totals $(\Pi_1, \Pi_2, \Pi_3, \Pi_4) = (1, 1, 1, 1)$; class sizes $(2, 2, 1, 1)$, so the true class weights are $W = (2, 2, 1, 1)$ and $\mu = 7/6$. (b) [The minimum of (7), over the whole box.] (7) is $\min\{(W_2 + 2W_3 + 3W_4)/(W_1 + W_2 + W_3 + W_4) : 1 \leqslant W_j \leqslant 2\}$, and for every $W$ in the box $\dfrac{W_2 + 2W_3 + 3W_4}{W_1+W_2+W_3+W_4} - \dfrac76 = \dfrac{7(2 - W_1) + (2 - W_2) + 5(W_3 - 1) + 11(W_4 - 1)}{6(W_1+W_2+W_3+W_4)} \geqslant 0$, with equality exactly at $W = (2, 2, 1, 1)$. So $\mu_- = 7/6$, attained at the threshold vector with cut $k = 2$. (c) [The cut point.] The corrected rule (P025-T4) gives $k_- = 2$: $G^{-}_0 = 6/4 = 3/2 > y_{(1)} = 0$; $G^{-}_1 = (2\cdot 0 + 1 + 2 + 3)/(2 + 3) = 6/5 > y_{(2)} = 1$; $G^{-}_2 = (2(0+1) + 2 + 3)/(2\cdot 2 + 2) = 7/6 \leqslant y_{(3)} = 2$. (d) [The printed display at this cut.] With $k_- = 2$ the printed second sums run over $j = 1, \ldots, 4$: $\dfrac{2(0 + 1) + (0 + 1 + 2 + 3)}{2(1 + 1) + (1 + 1 + 1 + 1)} = \dfrac88 = 1 \neq \dfrac76$. The display with tails from $j = k_- + 1 = 3$ gives $\dfrac{2(0+1) + (2+3)}{2(1+1) + (1+1)} = \dfrac76$. (e) [With the printed cut-point rule as well.] The printed rule for $k_-$ (with $\geqslant$) gives $k_- = 0$ here ($3/2 \geqslant 0$), and then the printed lower limit is $j = -1$, which is not a class index: the display has no value.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix, proof of Proposition 1 (the implication on p. 239 and the display 'Thus $k^{\mathrm H} = \min\{\ldots\} = \min\{\ldots\}$' on p. 240), and (B1)-(B2) in the Supplement's proof of Proposition 2, corrected: the case $\gamma = 1$ treated separately
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected proof steps; the printed ones are transcribed in P025-T12. Sol's smallest repair, validated.json, P025-E004: 'At the start of the affected proofs, treat alpha=beta (gamma=1) separately: the weight boxes are singletons, giving the sample mean in Proposition 1 and the population mean in (6)-(7). Retain the proposition's cutoff convention to label the identical vector; do not equate it to the first stationary index in this case. Run the appendix's increment/minimum equivalence only for gamma>1 and the supplement's (B1)-(B2) strict-improvement argument only for alpha<beta. After the split, "if and only if" may replace "implies that", but that wording change alone is insufficient.']

(A) [Appendix, proof of Proposition 1.] Let $n \geqslant 1$, $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$, $0 < \alpha \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, $\gamma = \beta/\alpha$; for $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n$ let $w^k = (1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta, 1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$ with the first $k$ entries $1/\beta$ and the last $n-k$ entries $1/\alpha$, and $F_k = (w^{k\prime}y)/(w^{k\prime}1_n) = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i}{k + \gamma(n-k)}$. (A1) [Increment identity, every $\gamma \geqslant 1$.] For $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1$: $F_{k+1} - F_k = \dfrac{(1-\gamma)(y_{k+1} - F_k)}{k + 1 + \gamma(n-k-1)}$. (A2) [Case $\gamma = 1$.] Then $\alpha = \beta$, the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$ is the single point $(1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$, every $w^k$ equals it, $F_k = \bar y = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i/n$ for every $k$, and $\hat\mu^{\mathrm H} = \hat\mu^{\mathrm L} = \bar y$. The cut point of Proposition 1, $k^{\mathrm H} = \min\{0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1 : \bar y \leqslant y_{k+1}\}$, exists (because $\bar y \leqslant y_n$), and (4) holds with value $\bar y$; it is not claimed to equal $\min\{k : F_k \geqslant F_{k+1}\}$, which is $0$. (A3) [Case $\gamma > 1$.] For $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1$: $F_{k+1} - F_k \leqslant 0$ if and only if $F_k \leqslant y_{k+1}$. If $F_k \leqslant y_{k+1}$ and $k + 2 \leqslant n$, then $F_{k+1} \leqslant y_{k+1} \leqslant y_{k+2}$. Consequently $k^{\mathrm H} = \min\{0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1 : F_k \geqslant F_{k+1}\} = \min\{0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1 : F_k \leqslant y_{k+1}\}$, and $F_{k^{\mathrm H}} = \max_{0 \leqslant k \leqslant n} F_k$.

(B) [Supplement, proof of Proposition 2.] Let $a = 1/\beta \leqslant b = 1/\alpha$, $p = \Pi_k > 0$, $q = \Pi_{k+1} > 0$, $u = y_{(k)} < v = y_{(k+1)}$, $c_1 \in \mathbb{R}$, $c_2 \geqslant 0$, $\mu(x, z) = \dfrac{c_1 + x p u + z q v}{c_2 + x p + z q}$, $E_1 = c_2 u - c_1 + a q (u - v)$ and $E_2 = c_1 - c_2 v + b p (u - v)$ (the left sides of (B1) and (B2)), and $D_{xz} = c_2 + x p + z q > 0$. (B-i) [Exact identities.] $D_{aa}D_{ba}\{\mu(a, a) - \mu(b, a)\} = (a - b)\,p\,E_1$ and $D_{bb}D_{ba}\{\mu(b, b) - \mu(b, a)\} = (a - b)\,q\,E_2$. (B-ii) [As printed.] $E_1 + E_2 = (c_2 + b p + a q)(u - v) < 0$. (B-iii) [Case $\alpha < \beta$.] $\mu(1/\beta, 1/\beta) > \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$ if and only if (B1), and $\mu(1/\alpha, 1/\alpha) > \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$ if and only if (B2); by (B-ii) at least one of the two strict improvements holds. (B-iv) [Case $\alpha = \beta = c$.] Every $\pi_i = c$, $\Pi_j = c|\Upsilon_j|$, the box is the single point $W_j = 1/c$, and (6) and (7) both equal $\sum_j |\Upsilon_j| y_{(j)}/\sum_j |\Upsilon_j| = \mu$; both differences in (B-i) are $0$ whatever the signs of $E_1$, $E_2$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: (S1)-(S3) of the standing assumptions: the sample $y_1 \leqslant \cdots \leqslant y_n$, the Hajek estimator (1) $\hat\mu = w'y/(w'1_n)$ with $w_i = \pi_i^{-1}$, the bounds $0 < \alpha \leqslant \pi_i \leqslant \beta \leqslant 1$, the problems (2) and (3) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^n$, and $\gamma = \beta/\alpha \geqslant 1$ [all p. 235-236 (PDF pp. 1-2)]. (S4)-(S5) of the standing assumptions: $Y$, $y_{(1)} < \cdots < y_{(|Y|)}$, $\Upsilon_j$, $\Pi_j = \sum_{i\in\Upsilon_j}\pi_i$, $W_j \equiv |\Upsilon_j|/\Pi_j$, the identity $\mu = \sum_j W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}/\sum_j W_j\Pi_j$, and the problems (6) and (7) over the box $[1/\beta, 1/\alpha]^{|Y|}$ [all p. 237 (PDF p. 3)]. [Appendix, p. 239 (PDF p. 5)] 'Given the structure of $w^{\mathrm H}$, it remains to show that the optimal objective value of (2) is (4). The first-order condition for $k^{\mathrm H}$ to maximize (2) can be characterized as follows. Let $w^k = (1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta, 1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$ where the first $k$ entries are $1/\beta$ and the last $n - k$ are $1/\alpha$. Then $(w^{k+1\prime}y)/(w^{k+1\prime}1_n) - (w^{k\prime}y)/(w^{k\prime}1_n) \leqslant 0$ implies that $\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i}{k + \gamma(n-k)} \leqslant y_{k+1}$. If $(w^{k\prime}y)/(w^{k\prime}1_n) \geqslant (w^{k+1\prime}y)/(w^{k+1\prime}1_n)$, then $(w^{k+1\prime}y)/(w^{k+1\prime}1_n) \geqslant (w^{k+2\prime}y)/(w^{k+2\prime}1_n)$ since $\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+2}^{n} y_i}{k+1+\gamma(n-k-1)} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i + (1-\gamma)y_{k+1}}{k+1+\gamma(n-k-1)} \leqslant \dfrac{[k+\gamma(n-k)]y_{k+1} + (1-\gamma)y_{k+1}}{k+1+\gamma(n-k-1)} = y_{k+1} \leqslant y_{k+2}$.' [Appendix, p. 240 (PDF p. 6)] 'Thus $k^{\mathrm H} = \min\left\{k \geqslant 0 : \dfrac{w^{k\prime}y}{w^{k\prime}1_n} \geqslant \dfrac{w^{k+1\prime}y}{w^{k+1\prime}1_n}\right\} = \min\left\{k \geqslant 0 : \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} y_i + \gamma\sum_{i=k+1}^{n} y_i}{k + \gamma(n-k)} \leqslant y_{k+1}\right\}$. The solution to (3) can be derived in a similar manner.' [Supplement, proof of Proposition 2, pp. 1-2] 'The structure of this vertex solution is of the form $W_+ = (1/\beta, \ldots, 1/\beta, 1/\alpha, \ldots, 1/\alpha)$ where the first $k_+ \geq 0$ entries are $1/\beta$ and the last $|Y| - k_+$ are $1/\alpha$. To see this, assume that there exists $\{(W_+)_k, (W_+)_{k+1}\} = (1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$. We will show that replacing the value of the pair with either $(1/\beta, 1/\beta)$ or $(1/\alpha, 1/\alpha)$ will lead to an objective value for (6) that is strictly larger. Define $c_1 \equiv \sum_{j\neq\{k,k+1\}} W_j\Pi_j y_{(j)}$, $c_2 \equiv \sum_{j\neq\{k,k+1\}} W_j\Pi_j$, and $\mu(W_k, W_{k+1}) \equiv \dfrac{c_1 + W_k\Pi_k y_{(k)} + W_{k+1}\Pi_{k+1}y_{(k+1)}}{c_2 + W_k\Pi_k + W_{k+1}\Pi_{k+1}}$. Then the condition $\mu(1/\beta, 1/\beta) > \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$ is equivalent to $c_2 y_{(k)} - c_1 + \beta^{-1}\Pi_{k+1}(y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)}) < 0$ (B1) and the condition $\mu(1/\alpha, 1/\alpha) > \mu(1/\alpha, 1/\beta)$ is equivalent to $c_1 - c_2 y_{(k+1)} + \alpha^{-1}\Pi_k(y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)}) < 0$. (B2) The assertion is true if either (B1) or (B2) holds. To show this, observe that the sum of the left hand sides of (B1) and (B2) is negative, so at least one of them has to be negative: $\{c_2 y_{(k)} - c_1 + \beta^{-1}\Pi_{k+1}(y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)})\} + \{c_1 - c_2 y_{(k+1)} + \alpha^{-1}\Pi_k(y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)})\} = (c_2 + \alpha^{-1}\Pi_k + \beta^{-1}\Pi_{k+1})\{y_{(k)} - y_{(k+1)}\} < 0$.' Conventions (S7): empty sums are $0$; cut-point rules range over the $k$ for which the next outcome is defined; $F^{\mathrm H}_k$, $F^{\mathrm L}_k$, $G^{+}_k$, $G^{-}_k$ as in (S7c).
